Dedicated in June 1976, the Sister Cities Plaza, a site of 0.5 acres (2,000 m2) located at 18th and Benjamin Franklin Parkway, honors Philadelphia's relationships with Tel Aviv and Florence which were its first sister cities. Another landmark, the Torun Triangle, honoring the sister city relationship with Torun, Poland, was constructed in 1976, west of the United Way building at 18th Street and the Benjamin Franklin Parkway. In addition, the Triangle contains the Copernicus monument. Renovations were made to Sister Cities Park in mid-2011 and on May 10, 2012, SCP was reopened and currently features an interactive fountain honoring Philadelphia's ten sister and friendship cities, a cafe and visitor's center, children's play area, outdoor garden, and boat pond, as well as pavilion built to environmentally friendly standards.

The theater says the incident was a misunderstanding and was not political in nature. On August 31, a Russian court sentenced two members of the Kazan theater group "School of Drama" to 20 days in jail for performing a play about the Russian revolutionary leader Vladimir Lenin in a cemetery. Harvard's athletic rivalry with Yale is intense in every sport in which they meet, coming to a climax each fall in the annual football meeting, which dates back to 1875 and is usually called simply "The Game." While Harvard's football team is no longer one of the country's best as it often was a century ago during football's early days (it won the Rose Bowl in 1920), both it and Yale have influenced the way the game is played. In 1903, Harvard Stadium introduced a new era into football with the first-ever permanent reinforced concrete stadium of its kind in the country. The stadium's structure actually played a role in the evolution of the college game. Seeking to reduce the alarming number of deaths and serious injuries in the sport, Walter Camp (former captain of the Yale football team), suggested widening the field to open up the game. But the stadium was too narrow to accommodate a wider playing surface. So, other steps had to be taken. Camp would instead support revolutionary new rules for the 1906 season. These included legalizing the forward pass, perhaps the most significant rule change in the sport's history.

Beginners and experts alike can make important discoveries, though they may do so in different ways and for different reasons. While beginners bring a fresh perspective and an open mind unencumbered by established beliefs, experts have a wealth of knowledge and experience that allows them to build on what has come before. In science, beginners are more likely to stumble upon discoveries by accident or make connections that others have missed precisely because they lack preconceptions about what is possible or probable. Their minds are open and unrestrained by dogma. However, experts are better equipped to interpret surprising results or recognize the significance of an unforeseen finding. They can design more sophisticated experiments or observations to explore new phenomena and understand their implications. Many important discoveries are the result of collaboration between beginners and experts, or experts who retain a beginner's sense of curiosity and imagination. In art and culture, beginners are more apt to innovate simply because they are less bound by convention or tradition. They may stumble upon a new technique, combine genres in an unprecedented way, or draw inspiration from unexpected sources. However, it is often the experts - those with a deep understanding of the historical context and technical skills honed through long practice - who recognize, mentor, and promote new talent. They are also best positioned to build upon cultural traditions by introducing subtle variations or making references that only other experts may appreciate. While beginners and experts each have advantages for discovery, the dichotomy between them is often overstated. In reality, people move back and forth across this spectrum as they gain experience in a field. Maintaining a beginner's mindset of openness and wonder, even after years or decades of work, is what allows for continued growth and the possibility of new insights. The most profound discoveries are usually made by those with a wealth of knowledge who never quite lose the beginner's impulse to question assumptions and imagine what might be possible beyond the current horizon of understanding. With open yet disciplined inquiry, beginners and experts alike can reveal new truths about ourselves and the world around us.

Travis Hirschi’s Social Bond Theory Essay When approaching human social behavior, scholars have generated several theories that propose specific elements of behavioral influences. One of such theories is the Social Bond Theory introduced by Travis Hirschi. The essence of his theoretical approach is that all people are inherently inclined to engage in delinquent behaviors, and particular social bonds constrain or reinforce criminal behaviors. Four essential social bonds, namely attachment, commitment, involvement, and belief, are the driving forces of either pro-social or anti-social behavior. Firstly, attachment is a type of social bond characterized by close relationships with the members of a group to which one belongs. Family is such an attachment source, on which individuals depend and whose influence regulates their decision-making (Zaidi, 2016). The second bond is a belief system through which one’s religious views and values are developed. The strengths of religious beliefs regulate behavior, thus inducing either pro- or anti-social behavior. The third social bond component is involvement in conventional activities, characterized by the regularity of displaying conventional social behaviors as dictated by a group with whom one associates. For example, involvement in education might be a factor for maintaining pro-social behavior and minimizing the risks for delinquency (Zaidi, 2016). Lastly, commitment is the final social bond that characterizes the level of one’s likelihood to follow conventional norms of social behavior. The more individual is committed to lows and norms, the less they are likely to engage in unlawful behaviors. In conclusion, the Social Bond Theory elements demonstrate that the effect of the factors within individuals’ attachment, beliefs, involvement, and commitment predetermine their behavior in society. The acceptance of law violating behaviors might derive from a person’s belonging to a group where social norms are not followed and are not included in the belief system. The weaker one’s attachment, involvement, and commitment with conventional law-abiding activities, the more likely he or she is to commit crimes. Reference Zaidi, A. U., Couture-Carron, A., & Maticka-Tyndale, E. (2016). ‘Should I or should I not’?: An exploration of South Asian youth’s resistance to cultural deviancy. A CO2 scrubber is a device that removes carbon dioxide (CO2) from the air or other gases. It works by using a chemical process to capture the CO2 and separate it from the other gases. Here's how it works: The gas (usually air) containing CO2 is passed through a scrubber. Inside the scrubber, there is a chemical solution called a "scrubbing solution" that is used to absorb the CO2. The CO2 is attracted to the chemical solution and sticks to it, similar to how a magnet sticks to metal. As the gas passes through the scrubber, more and more CO2 is absorbed by the scrubbing solution. The scrubber is designed so that the chemical solution stays in one place while the gas flows through it. This helps to make sure that as much CO2 as possible is removed from the gas. Once the gas has passed through the scrubber, it is much cleaner and has much less CO2 in it. CO2 scrubbers are used in a variety of applications, including air purification, greenhouse gas reduction, and the production of beverages. They can be small and portable, or large and stationary, depending on the needs of the user.

There are a couple of really big drawbacks to the hydrogen car with current technology. The first is hydrogen storage. Although hydrogen has a terrific energy density for it's weight (1 pound of hydrogen has 3x the energy of 1 pound of gasoline) It turns out that as a gas and not a liquid, storing it is difficult and the space that the hydrogen takes up (the volume) is much much larger than the same amount of gasoline. While we can put more hydrogen in a smaller volume, that increases the pressure and is very dangerous when you want to be able to drive a car for more than a few miles without refilling. The second problem comes from difficulty of getting hydrogen. It turns out that we get a lot of our hydrogen from oil right now, producing carbon dioxide just as much as if we burned the oil as gasoline. So in the end, it doesn't make a lot of sense to use hydrogen as an alternative to gas and oil right now. That said, there are a lot of people working on ways to store hydrogen gas safely and produce it from water using solar electricity, which has only oxygen as a waste product.

The Battle of Worth (also known as Froschwiller or Reichshoffen) began when the two armies clashed again on 6 August near Worth in the town of Froschwiller, about 10 miles (16 km) from Wissembourg. The Crown Prince of Prussia's 3rd army had, on the quick reaction of his Chief of Staff General von Blumenthal, drawn reinforcements which brought its strength up to 140,000 troops. The French had been slowly reinforced and their force numbered only 35,000. Although badly outnumbered, the French defended their position just outside Froschwiller. By afternoon, the Germans had suffered c.10,500 killed or wounded and the French had lost a similar number of casualties and another c.9,200 men taken prisoner, a loss of about 50. The Germans captured Froschwiller which sat on a hilltop in the centre of the French line. Having lost any hope for victory and facing a massacre, the French army disengaged and retreated in a westerly direction towards Bitche and Saverne, hoping to join French forces on the other side of the Vosges mountains. The German 3rd army did not pursue the French but remained in Alsace and moved slowly south, attacking and destroying the French garrisons in the vicinity.

The High Middle Ages was a period of great religious movements. Besides the Crusades and monastic reforms, people sought to participate in new forms of religious life. New monastic orders were founded, including the Carthusians and the Cistercians. The latter especially expanded rapidly in their early years under the guidance of Bernard of Clairvaux (d. 1153). These new orders were formed in response to the feeling of the laity that Benedictine monasticism no longer met the needs of the laymen, who along with those wishing to enter the religious life wanted a return to the simpler hermetical monasticism of early Christianity, or to live an Apostolic life. Religious pilgrimages were also encouraged. Old pilgrimage sites such as Rome, Jerusalem, and Compostela received increasing numbers of visitors, and new sites such as Monte Gargano and Bari rose to prominence.

Dear Senator, I am writing to you today to express my support for abolishing the Electoral College and electing the President of the United States by popular vote. The Electoral College is an outdated system that no longer reflects the will of the people. In recent elections, candidates have won the popular vote but lost the presidency due to the Electoral College. This is undemocratic and unfair to the majority of voters. There are several reasons why I believe the Electoral College should be abolished. Nirst, it gives too much power to a few states. In 2016, Donald Trump won the presidency with only 304 electoral votes, despite losing the popular vote by over 3 million votes. This is because Trump won a majority of votes in a few key swing states, such as Ohio and Florida. Second, the Electoral College discourages voter participation. Voters in states that are considered to be "safe" for one party or the other often feel that their vote does not matter. This is because the candidate who will win the electoral votes in that state is already a foregone conclusion. Third, the Electoral College is a relic of the past. It was created in the 18th century when the United States was a very different country. At that time, communication and travel were much slower, and it was difficult for people to vote in a national election. The Electoral College was designed as a way to ensure that all states had a voice in the election of the President. However, in the 21st century, there is no longer any need for the Electoral College. Communication and travel are much faster, and it is easy for people to vote in a national election. There is no reason why the President of the United States should not be elected by the popular vote of all eligible voters. I urge you to support legislation that would abolish the Electoral College and elect the President of the United States by popular vote. This would be a major step forward for democracy in the United States. Thank you for your time. Sincerely, [Your Name]

Seeking multiple opinions when making an important decision or asking for advice can help someone make a better choice for a few key reasons: First, getting perspectives from different people allows you to hear a wider range of ideas and options. No single person will have thought of every possible angle or consideration related to an issue. By talking to more than one person, you gain access to a broader collection of solutions, recommendations, and factors to weigh. This exposes you to alternatives you may not have thought of on your own. Secondly, multiple viewpoints help test the quality of a choice by exposing its weaknesses from additional vantage points. A decision that sounds perfect coming from one person may overlook some potential downsides or objections. Bouncing an idea off others reveals additional pros and cons you need to take into account before committing. Their thoughtful questions and prudent warnings about unforeseen consequences can prevent disastrous outcomes down the road. Third, seeking multiple opinions improves the choice by serving as a check against personal biases. Then emotionally invested in a decision, it's easy for our own judgments to become clouded or for unimportant personal preferences to skew our perspective. Consulting others removes some subjectivity, as they look at the situation more objectively and may notice fallacies in reasoning that we miss due to biases. A diversity of advisors balances individual partializes with external rationality. In addition, hearing a unanimous consensus from multiple trustworthy sources of advice significantly increases confidence that a choice is solid and well supported. One person could be wrong or make a questionable recommendation, but several agreeing opinions reduce the margin of error and uncertainty. The synchronization of guidance reassures that after considering various angles, the conclusion is likely to be a prudent one. For these important reasons, seeking advice from more than just one individual can help someone choose the best path by drawing on a richer set of knowledge, testing ideas from different angles, improving critical thinking through an objective outsider perspective, and boosting confidence with consistent external recommendations. Making any decision with such a multifaceted process and diverse Set of inputs will lead to wiser and higher quality results.

We consider the problem of detecting anomalies among a given set of processes using their noisy binary sensor measurements. The noiseless sensor measurement corresponding to a normal process is 0, and the measurement is 1 if the process is anomalous. The decision-making algorithm is assumed to have no knowledge of the number of anomalous processes. The algorithm is allowed to choose a subset of the sensors at each time instant until the confidence level on the decision exceeds the desired value. Our objective is to design a sequential sensor selection policy that dynamically determines which processes to observe at each time and when to terminate the detection algorithm. The selection policy is designed such that the anomalous processes are detected with the desired confidence level while incurring minimum cost which comprises the delay in detection and the cost of sensing. We cast this problem as a sequential hypothesis testing problem within the framework of Markov decision processes, and solve it using the actor-critic deep reinforcement learning algorithm. This deep neural network-based algorithm offers a low complexity solution with good detection accuracy. We also study the effect of statistical dependence between the processes on the algorithm performance. Through numerical experiments, we show that our algorithm is able to adapt to any unknown statistical dependence pattern of the processes.

Nowadays, governments are facing difficult decisions when it comes to allocating their funds. One such decision is whether to invest in building theaters and sports stadiums or to focus more spending on medical care and education. Jhile there is no straightforward answer to this question, this essay will provide arguments for why governments should prioritize medical care and education over theaters and sports stadiums. First, medical care and education are necessities for the healthy functioning and wellbeing of society. Medical care is essential for protecting and preserving the health of citizens, and a well educated population is necessary for fostering economic and social progress. In contrast, theaters and sports stadiums provide luxuries rather than necessities. This means that if the budget is limited, governments should prioritize medical care and education over theaters and sports stadiums. Furthermore, investment in medical care and education can create long term benefits that far exceed the short term benefits of investing in theaters and sports stadiums. For instance, investing in a new hospital or school can provide a lasting benefit to the local community, including improved access to quality healthcare and a better educated population. By contrast, the benefits of investing in a theater or a sports stadium are likely to be much more short term, since people will eventually lose interest and move onto something else. Finally, investing in medical care and education can help to reduce inequality within society. By investing in quality healthcare, governments can ensure that everyone has access to the medical treatment they need, regardless of their income. Similarly, investing in education can help to reduce the disparities in educational attainment among different social classes. By contrast, investing in theaters and sports stadiums only serves to benefit wealthier members of society, since they are more likely to be able to afford tickets to these events. In conclusion, when governments are faced with difficult decisions regarding the allocation of their funds, they should prioritize medical care and education over theaters and sports stadiums. This is because medical care and education are necessities rather than luxuries, their benefits can create long term benefits, and they can help to reduce inequality within society.

String theory is one of the most promising candidates for a theory that unifies quantum mechanics and general relativity. It proposes that the fundamental building blocks of matter are not point particles but tiny vibrating strings. These strings vibrate in different ways, and each vibrational pattern appears as a different elementary particle like electrons, quarks, photons, etc. So, all matter in the universe, from the smallest particle to the largest galaxy, would arise from the different vibrational patterns of these fundamental strings. String theory also posits that there are 10 or 11 dimensions of space-time, most of which are invisible to us. The strings can vibrate in all of these dimensions, while we only perceive the three spatial dimensions that we observe. The other dimensions are “compactified” at very small scales, curled up invisibly. String theory is an elegant theory that provides a framework for unifying quantum mechanics and general relativity into a theory of quantum gravity. However, it is not yet a complete theory, and it is difficult to test because the strings are so small and the extra dimensions invisible. String theory started in the late 1960s and early 1970s as physicists were trying to understand the strong nuclear force. They proposed that hadrons could be modeled as vibrating strings instead of point particles. This early version evolved into string theory as a possible theory of quantum gravity. In the 1980s, string theorists showed that the strings required six extra dimensions of space for mathematical consistency. They also found that string theory did not describe just the strong force, but it could incorporate all the forces and all types of particles in one theory. In the 1990s and 2000s, string theorists developed M-theory, which proposes 11 dimensions of space-time and contains strings as well as other objects like membranes. M-theory helped unite various versions of string theory and provided more insights into how strings work. However, string theory remains highly mathematical and speculative. While it is promising, more work is needed to determine if it matches our physical reality. Experiments at high-energy particle accelerators may eventually yield evidence to support or contradict string theory. Whatever the outcome, string theory has led to many insights and pushed physics into new realms of understanding in the quest for a theory of everything.

The essay under discussion centers around the concept of scientific variables, which are essential components in any research. These variables are empirical phenomena that exhibit dynamic behavior by assuming different values or intensities based on various factors. Their significance is undeniable, as they serve as the basis for collecting data that is crucial for analyzing behavioral patterns. Consequently, understanding the nature of scientific variables and their applications in research is vital for anyone pursuing a career in the scientific field. Scientific variables can be further classified into different categories based on their characteristics. For instance, independent variables are the factors that are deliberately manipulated by the researcher to observe the effects on the dependent variables. These variables can either be continuous or discrete, with the former being subject to change over a range of values, and the latter having a limited number of possible values. Another significant category of scientific variables is the control variables, which are used to minimize the influence of extraneous factors on the outcome of a study. By controlling these variables, researchers can ensure that any observed changes in the dependent variables are a direct result of the manipulation of independent variables. Moreover, moderator variables play a pivotal role in determining the strength and direction of the relationship between independent and dependent variables. These variables can either enhance or weaken the effect of independent variables on the dependent variables, thereby affecting the outcome of research. Apart from the aforementioned categories, there are also intervening variables, which are introduced by the researcher to influence the relationship between independent and dependent variables. These variables can either be manipulated or observed by the researcher, depending on the research question. In conclusion, scientific variables are indispensable in the realm of research, as they provide the necessary data for analyzing behavioral patterns. Understanding the various categories of scientific variables, their characteristics, and their applications in research is essential for anyone pursuing a career in the scientific field. By delving deeper into this topic, we can gain a better appreciation of the complexity and intricacies involved in conducting scientific research, ultimately contributing to the advancement of knowledge in various disciplines.

Social innovation and urban transformation are deeply interconnected. As new ideas emerge in cities that improve lives, the physical landscape inevitably shifts in response. This relationship is symbiotic - social innovations depend on the unique conditions of cities to spread and scale, while cities rely on innovation to thrive, adapt to change, and meet the needs of citizens. Cities have always been hubs of innovation due to their density and diversity. When people from wide-ranging backgrounds converge in large numbers, new ideas collide and combine in unexpected ways. The proximity of housing and workspaces also allows for more interactions and collaborations, as people can easily connect face-to-face. These interactions across sectors and social groups facilitate the spread of knowledge and the cross-pollination of ideas that spur innovation. At the same time, the challenges of urban life demand new solutions. Overcrowding, poverty, pollution, and other issues create pressures that drive people to come up with fresh ideas to improve their communities. Grassroots movements emerge to tackle problems in new ways when existing institutions and governments fail to help. Community organizations form, non-profits are created, and social enterprises develop to fill these gaps through innovative means. As social innovations take hold, they dramatically transform the fabric of cities. New public transit systems overhaul infrastructure, green spaces replace abandoned lots, fresh food finds its way into food deserts, and civic engagement blossoms. Each of these changes in turn enhances the conditions for further innovation. More interconnected transit opens up opportunities for interaction, community gardens foster social cohesion, and engaged citizens are empowered to identify and solve the next set of pressing challenges. In rapidly globalizing and urbanizing societies, this relationship between social innovation and urban transformation is increasingly crucial. With over half the world's population now in cities, finding ways to meet people's needs, build resilience, and improve lives depends on the combined forces of grassroots ingenuity and a willingness to reinvent outdated systems. At their best, cities that nurture innovation can thrive through continuous self-renewal, evolving in harmony with the creative solutions generated within them. Social innovation and urban transformation together hold the key to sustainable, just, and prosperous cities of the future.

The Facial Action Coding System, or FACS, is a method for analyzing and categorizing facial expressions. Developed by Dr. Paul Ekman and Dr. Wallace V. Friesen, it serves as an objective way to understand human emotions. FACS is comprised of 43 action units, which are specific movements of facial muscles. These action units are organized into six main categories or "emotion families": happiness, sadness, anger, contempt, fear, and surprise. Each emotion family has its own set of action units, and the combination of these units creates various facial expressions that can be observed in everyday interactions. The FACS is a useful tool for researchers and psychologists, as it provides a standard language for discussing and studying facial expressions. It can help in understanding cultural differences in emotional displays and identifying emotional disorders like facial paralysis or facial blinding, which might affect an individual's ability to communicate their emotions through facial expressions. In summary, the Facial Action Coding System is a systematic method of analyzing and categorizing human emotions based on specific facial movements. It consists of 43 action units grouped into six emotion families and has various applications in understanding human emotions and emotional disorders.

A 2010 study by Bray et al., using SNP microarray techniques and linkage analysis found that when assuming Druze and Palestinian Arab populations to represent the reference to world Jewry ancestor genome, between 35 to 55 percent of the modern Ashkenazi genome can possibly be of European origin, and that European "admixture is considerably higher than previous estimates by studies that used the Y chromosome" with this reference point. Assuming this reference point the linkage disequilibrium in the Ashkenazi Jewish population was interpreted as "matches signs of interbreeding or 'admixture' between Middle Eastern and European populations." On the Bray et al. tree, Ashkenazi Jews were found to be a genetically more divergent population than Russians, Orcadians, French, Basques, Italians, Sardinians and Tuscans. The study also observed that Ashkenazim are more diverse than their Middle Eastern relatives, which was counterintuitive because Ashkenazim are supposed to be a subset, not a superset, of their assumed geographical source population. However, it's possible that the relaxation of marriage prescription in the ancestors of Ashkenazim that drove their heterozygosity up, while the maintenance of the FBD rule in native Middle Easterners have been keeping their heterozygosity values in check. Ashkenazim distinctiveness as found in the Bray et al. study, therefore, may come from their ethnic endogamy (ethnic inbreeding), which allowed them to "mine" their ancestral gene pool in the context of relative reproductive isolation from European neighbors, and not from clan endogamy (clan inbreeding). Consequently, their higher diversity compared to Middle Easterners stems from the latter's marriage practices, not necessarily from the former's admixture with Europeans.

While the Face on Mars might appear as a face to some people, it is important to recognize that it is just a product of the environment and natural forces. Although artificial neural networks have shown great promise in applications including computer vision and speech recognition, there remains considerable practical and theoretical difficulty in optimizing their parameters. The seemingly unreasonable task of predicting a given function (such as an image or text) from previously collected data has required the development of highly accurate learning models that can account for all possible inputs and noise. It is also desirable to approximate these functions with large numbers of neurons in order to maintain high-quality accuracy while using relatively small amounts of memory. Unfortunately, this often requires exponentially more storage space than would be necessary if input noise were completely ignored. In addition, the most popular methods are those based on linear predictive coding whose output characteristics are complicated by time-varying environmental conditions such as changes in lighting. It has long been recognized that the best way to implement many machine learning algorithms is through hierarchical structures. Heterogeneous architectures, i.e., where each layer implements its own tasks, allow higher levels of abstraction. This allows the algorithm to run at lower cost since it does not require startup time, high-level computations to determine which layers should execute, and time spent reevaluating that decision when new information arrives. However, how to design a hierarchy so that the evolving weights of individual layers match those predicted by one another remains a difficult problem.

Data Poisoning attacks involve an attacker modifying training data to maliciously control a model trained on this data. Previous poisoning attacks against deep neural networks have been limited in scope and success, working only in simplified settings or being prohibitively expensive for large datasets. In this work, we focus on a particularly malicious poisoning attack that is both "from scratch" and "clean label," meaning we analyze an attack that successfully works against new, randomly initialized models, and is nearly imperceptible to humans, all while perturbing only a small fraction of the training data. The central mechanism of this attack is matching the gradient direction of malicious examples. We analyze why this works, supplement with practical considerations. and show its threat to real-world practitioners, finding that it is the first poisoning method to cause targeted misclassification in modern deep networks trained from scratch on a full-sized, poisoned ImageNet dataset. Finally we demonstrate the limitations of existing defensive strategies against such an attack, concluding that data poisoning is a credible threat, even for large-scale deep learning systems.

Tensor decompositions are used in various data mining applications from social network to medical applications and are extremely useful in discovering latent structures or concepts in the data. Many real-world applications are dynamic in nature and so are their data. To deal with this dynamic nature of data, there exist a variety of online tensor decomposition algorithms. A central assumption in all those algorithms is that the number of latent concepts remains fixed throughout the entire stream. However, this need not be the case. Every incoming batch in the stream may have a different number of latent concepts, and the difference in latent concepts from one tensor batch to another can provide insights into how our findings in a particular application behave and deviate over time. In this paper, we define "concept" and "concept drift" in the context of streaming tensor decomposition, as the manifestation of the variability of latent concepts throughout the stream. Furthermore, we introduce SeekAndDestroy 1 1 footnote 1 The method name is after (and a tribute to) Metallica's song from their first album (who also owns the copyright for the name), an algorithm that detects concept drift in streaming tensor decomposition and is able to produce results robust to that drift. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that investigates concept drift in streaming tensor decomposition. We extensively evaluate SeekAndDestroy on synthetic datasets, which exhibit a wide variety of realistic drift. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of SeekAndDestroy , both in the detection of concept drift and in the alleviation of its effects, producing results with similar quality to decomposing the entire tensor in one shot. Additionally, in real datasets, SeekAndDestroy outperforms other streaming baselines, while discovering novel useful components.

For millenia humans were hunters and gatherers. We moved from place to place and ate the plants and animals that grew there. Then, the neolithic revolution happened. We figured out how to harness fire for cooking, make pottery and other things so we could grow our own food and store it in caves or houses. As more people started doing this, civilization developed - agriculture (growing crops), cities, writing, roads, these were all developments of a much larger population base. This is where you get into the debate about whether technological progress or the expansion of the human race caused us as a species to advance faster than natural selection would have allowed naturally: "The population explosion was an important part of the transition, but not necessarily if you think that large populations are a countervailing factor against evolutionary change; rather, I think they are a driving force towards it. If you have a very low-population world with lots of genetic diversity among its members, then evolution will be slower because it won't need to weed out bad mutants - it'll just let them develop, survive and reproduce at their current rate until overshoot causes some sort of catastrophe. By contrast, when you add genetic variation, mutations can occur randomly and drift through populations without being eliminated by natural selection. And you don't even need mutation, sometimes small changes introduced during reproductive isolation will result in big breakthroughs. You might look today at a Western person who has brown eyes and say "that's really cool" and attribute that to skin pigmentation genetics, but it may instead come down to an animal protein adaptation in an ancestor several thousand years ago. So yes, a huge, increased human population helped bring about the Neolithic Revolution, but it came at a time when the environment wasn't changing significantly enough for selective pressures to act on us." - Daniel Lieberman Source: (Wired)

In unsupervised classification, Hidden Markov Models (HMM) are used to account for a neighborhood structure between observations. The emission distributions are often supposed to belong to some parametric family. In this paper, a semiparametric modeling where the emission distributions are a mixture of parametric distributions is proposed to get a higher flexibility. We show that the classical EM algorithm can be adapted to infer the model parameters. For the initialisation step, starting from a large number of components, a hierarchical method to combine them into the hidden states is proposed. Three likelihood-based criteria to select the components to be combined are discussed. To estimate the number of hidden states, BIC-like criteria are derived. A simulation study is carried out both to determine the best combination between the merging criteria and the model selection criteria and to evaluate the accuracy of classification. The proposed method is also illustrated using a biological dataset from the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana. A R package HMMmix is freely available on the CRAN.

Hardware acceleration refers to the use of computer hardware, specifically hardware designed to perform some functions more efficiently than is possible in software running on a general-purpose central processing unit (CPU). By using hardware acceleration, a computer can perform certain tasks faster and more efficiently than it could with just a CPU. Hardware acceleration is often used in graphics and video processing, as these tasks can be very resource-intensive and can benefit greatly from specialized hardware. For example, a graphics processing unit (GPU) is a type of hardware designed specifically to handle the complex calculations required to render images and video. By offloading these tasks to the GPU, the CPU is free to perform other tasks, resulting in improved overall performance. Hardware acceleration can also be used in other areas, such as data processing, encryption, and network communication. In these cases, specialized hardware such as a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) or an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) may be used to perform certain tasks more efficiently than a CPU. Overall, hardware acceleration can help to improve the performance and efficiency of a computer by taking advantage of specialized hardware designed to perform specific tasks faster and more efficiently than a general-purpose CPU.

The Electoral College also distorts the popular vote. In 2000, for example, Al Gore won the popular vote by over 500,000 votes, but lost the election to George W. The Electoral College has been the subject of debate and criticism since its establishment. It is a unique system designed to elect the United States President and Vice President. The main purpose of the Electoral College is to ensure representation of each state in the presidential election and maintain the balance between urban and rural populations. However, the system has faced various criticisms over the years, mainly due to its potential flaws. Some argue that the Electoral College favors less populous states, which results in a skewed representation of the country's overall population. Additionally, the Electoral College has produced some unexpected outcomes, like when a candidate wins the popular vote but loses the electoral vote. Another issue with the Electoral College is the possibility of a "faithless elector," an elector voting for someone other than the candidate chosen by the state. This can lead to unpredictable results and potential confusion in the election process. Despite its drawbacks, the Electoral College has been a part of American democracy for more than two centuries. It has helped ensure a stable transition of power between political administrations. The system has also been modified throughout its existence to address some of its shortcomings. The Twelfth Amendment, for example, was adopted in 1804 to clarify the process of electing the President and Vice President. The Electoral College is not perfect, but it does have its merits. It allows for a more even representation of states in the presidential election, prevents the influence of a few densely populated areas, and helps maintain the federalist nature of the country. The Electoral College is a vital component of American democracy that has been in use for centuries, but it is important to recognize its shortcomings and consider possible improvements to the system as time goes on.

The Tibetan Empire emerged in the 7th century, but with the fall of the empire the region soon divided into a variety of territories. The bulk of western and central Tibet (U-Tsang) was often at least nominally unified under a series of Tibetan governments in Lhasa, Shigatse, or nearby locations; these governments were at various times under Mongol and Chinese overlordship. The eastern regions of Kham and Amdo often maintained a more decentralized indigenous political structure, being divided among a number of small principalities and tribal groups, while also often falling more directly under Chinese rule after the Battle of Chamdo; most of this area was eventually incorporated into the Chinese provinces of Sichuan and Qinghai. The current borders of Tibet were generally established in the 18th century.

Or, they may have a specific, but temporary, reason for not wanting to go. In other situations, it seems that there's no specific reason the child doesn't want to go; rather he just gets into his "I don't wanna" mode and refuses to budge from this position (even when it would be in their own best interests). To help understand why children are so resistant at times like these, I take them through an exercise called the Why Game. This involves asking open-ended questions about what is going on inside of them during a particular situation or with regard to something we're talking about together as parents. Asking such questions can sometimes result in surprising answers! The key here isn't always getting kids to come up with elaborate reasons behind refusing something you've asked them do - although you might find yourself surprised by some of those responses too. Instead, my focus has been more around helping children communicate clearly how they feel during certain moments or events without feeling pressured by adults who tend to see things differently than our youth often do. So while adult motivations usually involve trying to encourage feelings of self confidence, patience, initiative etc., it is important to remember that whatever your end goal might ultimately seem to be right now, if done 'wrong' (e.g. pushing a reluctant youngster), then all one ends up doing is creating resistance toward change at any point later down the road which makes implementing further changes difficultimpossible altogether. That said...there will almost certainly indeed need to be continued reminding after initial requests made until the desired behavior takes hold whether its finishing homework, taking out trash, cleaning room, eating dinner etc.. You'll get better results though once your teenager realizes that Mom Dad aren't bad people for continually repeating themselves over time especially since many likely avoid conflict and instead prefer to continue avoiding problems indefinitely. Until your teen comes along and shows him herself capable enough to make smart decisions independently....they probably won't!!

The proton has a positive charge while the electron has a negative charge . Neutrons are neutral . Photons are given off as electromagnetic radiation . For the sake of simplicity lets talk about photons , electrons and their antiparticle , the positron . The electron and positron have the same properties except the positron has positive charge where the electron is negative . The easiest way to think about it is when 2 electrons are near , they exchange a photon . The photon acts like a little billiard ball . It pushes the electron that emitted the photon away , and the photon knocks into the other electron , pushing it away as well . This is repulsion . Attraction between an electron / positron is similar , but the resulting momentum pushes the particles towards each other instead . How you ask ? Uncertainty ! Uncertainty states that it is impossible to know 2 properties of a particle simultaneously with precision , since measuring one will affect the other . Attraction therefore contains an uncertainty in the position of either the photon or the other particles which makes it seem like the photon is coming from the other side of both the electron and positron . We can observe the momentum of these particles , but therefore can not know their position . That s electromagnetism in a nutshell . Anyone else can feel free to correct where I am off .

The most commonly given starting point for the Middle Ages is 476, first used by Bruni.[A] For Europe as a whole, 1500 is often considered to be the end of the Middle Ages, but there is no universally agreed upon end date. Depending on the context, events such as Christopher Columbus's first voyage to the Americas in 1492, the conquest of Constantinople by the Turks in 1453, or the Protestant Reformation in 1517 are sometimes used. English historians often use the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485 to mark the end of the period. For Spain, dates commonly used are the death of King Ferdinand II in 1516, the death of Queen Isabella I of Castile in 1504, or the conquest of Granada in 1492. Historians from Romance-speaking countries tend to divide the Middle Ages into two parts: an earlier "High" and later "Low" period. English-speaking historians, following their German counterparts, generally subdivide the Middle Ages into three intervals: "Early," "High," and "Late." In the 19th century, the entire Middle Ages were often referred to as the "Dark Ages,B] but with the adoption of these subdivisions, use of this term was restricted to the Early Middle Ages, at least among historians.

I 'm going to answer your bonus question about blood instead of the original question . Blood is has four major components in people : White blood cells ( called leukocytes ) , red blood cells ( called erythrocytes ) , platelets ( called thrombocytes ) , and plasma . White blood cells are one of your body 's major lines of defense . They literally swallow and destroy things like bacteria , old cells , cancer cells , etc . White blood cells are made by stem cells in your bone marrow . Red blood cells are the cells that carry oxygen from your lungs to the body , and bring carbon dioxide from the body to the lungs for exhalation . These cells are also made by stem cells in your bone marrow . Platelets are responsible for making your blood clot . They 're super sticky , so as they start to pile up on top of each other , they can close up a bleed and allow the tissue to regrow before being broken down or falling off . A scab is a classic example . These guys are made by a cell called the megakaryocyte ( also found in bone marrow , but not from the same cells the other blood cells are made from ) . Plasma is mostly water , but it also has some proteins , sugars , and minerals floating around in it . This is made mostly by you drinking water every day . All these parts are put together inside of your bones . Blood flows to the parts of your bones with blood vessels in them . The cells made in the marrow seep out into this blood , and the old , dying , and broken cells get picked up by the liver and broken down .

Gene expression programming (GEP) is a type of evolutionary computation method that is used to evolve computer programs or models. It is based on the principles of genetic programming, which uses a set of genetic-like operators to evolve solutions to problems. In GEP, the evolved solutions are represented as tree-like structures called expression trees. Each node in the expression tree represents a function or terminal, and the branches represent the arguments of the function. The functions and terminals in the expression tree can be combined in a variety of ways to form a complete program or model. To evolve a solution using GEP, a population of expression trees is first created. These trees are then evaluated according to some predefined fitness function, which measures how well the trees solve a particular problem. The trees that perform better are selected for reproduction, and new trees are created through a process of crossover and mutation. This process is repeated until a satisfactory solution is found. GEP has been used to solve a wide range of problems, including function approximation, symbolic regression, and classification tasks. It has the advantage of being able to evolve complex solutions using a relatively simple representation and set of operators, but it can be computationally intensive and may require fine-tuning to achieve good results.

A Belgian research group discovered a major security flaw in the keyless entry system of the Tesla Model X. The attack uses a device built from a Raspberry Pi computer and a cheap radio transmitter, which costs around 40. The attack works by intercepting the signals sent from the car to the key fob when it is used to unlock the doors. The attackers then use the Raspberry Pi to replay those signals, allowing them to open the car without having access to the actual key fob. Tesla has since released a software update to address the security flaw. The update requires owners to enter their unique PIN code each time they use the keyless entry system. This prevents attackers from using the same signal-spoofing technique to gain access to the vehicle. Tesla also recommends that owners keep their key fobs in a Faraday bag when not in use, which will block any malicious radio signals from being received by the key fob.

Community service is most valuable when people choose to volunteer of their own volition, because they care about making a positive impact. Forcing involvement could breed resentment rather than goodwill. That said, I do think developing a culture of service within the school is worthwhile. There are many options to encourage volunteerism without mandating it. For example, the school could regularly share opportunities to get involved with organizations in need of assistance. In Buddhism, karma refers to the concept of cause and effect. It is the idea that every action, whether physical or mental, has consequences that can affect the future of the person who performed the action.

According to the teachings of Buddhism, the consequences of an action are not necessarily determined by a higher power or deity, but rather by the natural laws of the universe. Every action creates a chain of events that can have positive or negative effects on the person who performed the action, as well as on those around them.

In Buddhist teachings, the consequences of an action are not limited to the present life, but can extend into future lives. This is because Buddhists believe in the concept of reincarnation, in which the consciousness of a person is reborn after death into a new body. Therefore, the actions and choices that a person makes in this life can have an impact on their future lives.

Karma is seen as a natural law, like the law of gravity. It is not a punishment or reward system imposed by a deity, but rather a consequence of one's actions. The goal in Buddhism is not to accumulate good karma, but rather to be mindful of one's actions and to cultivate a compassionate and caring attitude towards all beings, which can ultimately lead to a state of enlightenment.

At this point the OS must kill the process (usually via the task manager) by depriving it of its resources and forcefully killing off the game.', "Former game developer here, uMr-Magnus has the gist of it. Driverless cars are becoming an increasingly popular topic in the world of technology and transportation. While driverless cars have many potential benefits, there are also some challenges and concerns associated with their adoption. One of the main issues is the reliability of the technology itself. Autonomous cars must be able to function flawlessly in a wide range of conditions, including adverse weather, complex intersections, and unexpected obstacles. Additionally, there are questions surrounding the legal and ethical implications of driverless cars. For example, what happens if a driverless car needs to make a decision between potentially harming its occupants or pedestrians outside the vehicle? Despite these challenges and concerns, many automakers and technology companies are investing heavily in the development of driverless cars. In fact, several companies have already begun testing autonomous vehicles on public roads, with some even offering driverless car services. It is clear that driverless cars are the future of transportation, and their widespread adoption will undoubtedly change the way we travel, commute, and live.

You also have " electives , " which are credits that do n't exactly fit into the major track or the general education credits . This can lead to students simply memorizing information, rather than actually thinking about the material in a meaningful way. In conclusion, while technology can offer schools improved methods for instructing students, there are many drawbacks to their use in the classroom. The recently developed Deep Potential [Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 143001, 2018] is a powerful method to represent general inter-atomic potentials using deep neural networks. The success of Deep Potential rests on the proper treatment of locality and symmetry properties of each component of the network. In this paper, we leverage its network structure to effectively represent the mapping from the atomic configuration to the electron density in Kohn-Sham density function theory (KS-DFT). By directly targeting at the self-consistent electron density, we demonstrate that the adapted network architecture, called the Deep Density, can effectively represent the electron density as the linear combination of contributions from many local clusters. The network is constructed to satisfy the translation, rotation, and permutation symmetries, and is designed to be transferable to different system sizes. We demonstrate that using a relatively small number of training snapshots, Deep Density achieves excellent performance for one-dimensional insulating and metallic systems, as well as systems with mixed insulating and metallic characters. We also demonstrate its performance for real three-dimensional systems, including small organic molecules, as well as extended systems such as water (up to 512 molecules) and aluminum (up to 256 atoms).

Using Facial Action Coding System technology to read the emotional expressions of students in a classroom could potentially provide some benefits, but it also raises significant privacy concerns that make its overall value questionable. On one hand, this technology may help teachers gain insights into how their students are responding to lessons on an individual level. By detecting if students appear bored, confused, or engaged as class is ongoing, teachers could potentially make adjustments to improve instruction. This level of emotion detection could help ensure more students understand content and stay motivated to learn. The technology may also flag if a particular student seems distressed, allowing a teacher to check in on their wellbeing. However, continuously monitoring students' facial expressions without their consent crosses an ethical line. Classrooms are meant to be safe, inclusive environments for learning, not testing grounds for experimental technologies. Students should feel free to naturally express a range of emotions—including frustration with difficult concepts—without being subjected to computerized emotion surveillance. Even if data is supposedly anonymous, many students could still feel self-conscious under such monitoring, undermining their comfort at school. There are also concerns about accuracy and potential misinterpretation of data. Facial expression analysis is an imperfect science, so computers meant to detect emotions may misclassify students' responses. Teachers relying on this flawed data risk making incorrect assumptions about how students are processing lessons. Students could end up being unfairly judged or perceived in a way that does not truly reflect their experiences in class. Overall, while emotion detection technology hints at possible benefits, its application in classrooms raises serious problems related to student privacy, consent, and data reliability that are not easily solved. Unless such issues can be addressed through transparent safeguards that prioritize student well-being over experimental uses of technology, this surveillance threatens more harm than good to the learning environment. While the goals of insight into teaching and learning are worthwhile, this particular approach appears premature and potentially damaging without major changes.

Dear Senator, I am writing to you regarding the Electoral College system used in presidential elections in our state. I have researched and analyzed both sides of the argument regarding whether to retain the Electoral College or switch to a popular vote system. With the winner-takes-all system in most states, a candidate must win the majority of votes in a state to gain its entire electoral vote. This prevents the possibility of a close election where multiple states have split their votes and creates a clear winner. The Electoral College also forces candidates to have broad, transregional appeal. Candidates must appeal to voters in multiple states, not just those with the highest population, and this ensures that the president represents a diverse group of people. Furthermore, the Electoral College focuses attention on swing states. Candidates must spend time campaigning in these states, which are crucial for winning the election. This encourages candidates to address the concerns of voters in those states, and ultimately benefits the country as a whole. Additionally, the Electoral College balances the influence of large states. Without it, a candidate may focus only on highly populated areas and not address the concerns of smaller, rural areas. While some argue that the Electoral College is not a democratic system, it provides a stabilizing factor in our representative democratic process. The system ensures that the winner has a clear mandate to govern, and prevents the need for run-off elections. While there may be concerns about voter disenfranchisement in states dominated by a single party, the Electoral College provides a fair and balanced approach to electing our president. In conclusion, I strongly believe that our state should retain the Electoral College. The system provides a certain outcome, ensures broad representation, focuses attention on swing states, balances the influence of large states, and prevents voter disenfranchisement. Bitmessage is a decentralized, secure messaging system that allows people to send messages to each other without the need for a central server or authority. It uses a peer-to-peer network, similar to how BitTorrent or Bitcoin works, to transmit messages between users. Here's how it works in a nutshell: A user creates a message and selects a recipient by entering their Bitmessage address. The user's computer encrypts the message using the recipient's public key, which is a long string of numbers and letters that is unique to each user. This ensures that only the recipient can read the message. The encrypted message is broadcast to the Bitmessage network, which consists of many computers (called "nodes") that are running the Bitmessage software. The nodes on the network pass the message along to other nodes until it reaches the recipient. The recipient's computer receives the message and uses their private key (which is known only to them) to decrypt the message and read it. Bitmessage is designed to be very secure and private, as it uses advanced encryption techniques to ensure that only the intended recipient can read the message. It is also decentralized, which means that it does not rely on any central authority or server, making it resistant to censorship and tampering. I hope this helps to give you a better understanding of how Bitmessage works! If you have any further questions, please don't hesitate to ask.

The important role played by these structures requires their close proximity to each other; this is why they must be able to communicate with one another.

There are a few things to unpack in this prompt. First, it's important to understand the difference between competition and cooperation. Competition is defined as "the activity or condition of striving to gain or win something by defeating or establishing superiority over others" (Competition, n. D.). Cooperation, on the other hand, is defined as "the process of working together to the same end" (Cooperation, n. D.). With that in mind, it's important to note that competition and cooperation are not totally exclusive. In fact, they often go handstand. For example, in a team sport, players most cooperate in order to achieve the common goal of winning the game. However, they most also compete against the opposing team in order to do so. That said, there is merit to both competition and cooperation, and children should be taught both. Competition can teach children how to set and achieve goals, how to persevere in the face of adversity, and how to be gracious in victory and defeat. Cooperation, on the other hand, can teach children the value of teamwork, how to compromise, and how to communicate effectively. Both competition and cooperation are important life skills that children should learn. They are not totally exclusive, and both can be taught in a way that is beneficial to children.

A team from Glasgow University found there was a sharp fall in accidents from 5,901 in 1997 to 2,914 in 2014. The researchers said, however, there was "no evidence" the M74 had impacted on an "already decreasing trend." The five-mile (8km) route, which cost PS692m, links the M74 at Carmyle to the M8 southwest of the Kingston Bridge. Planning permission for the route was granted in October 1995 and immediately opposed by Joint Action Against the M74 (Jam74) - a coalition of community, environmental and sustainable transport groups. Construction began in 2008 after a last-ditch legal bid to halt the project was abandoned by Friends of the Earth Scotland and Jam74. Supporters claimed the road would bring economic benefits to the west of Scotland and help cut accidents, whereas critics argued it would cause more pollution, increase health problems and fragment communities. The Glasgow University study looked to evaluate the impact of the M74 extension on the number of road accidents on local roads during the construction period and following its opening. Lead author of the report, Dr Jonathan Olsen, said: "The building of the M74 extension in the south of Glasgow was controversial. There were strong arguments for and against its construction, but ultimately it went ahead. "One of the arguments in favour was that it could reduce road accidents on local streets. "In our study we examined police accident data from 1997 to 2014, three years after the new motorway was opened, and found that this predicted reduction in road accident numbers had not materialised." He added: "But on the other hand, we found no evidence that the M74 extension had led to an increase in accidents." Report co-author, Professor Rich Mitchell, added: "There is surprisingly little evidence about the impacts new motorways have. "This research will be useful for planners, politicians and residents elsewhere who are trying to decide whether to build or not." The study is published in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health.

While the idea of the "Face on Mars" being created by aliens is intriguing, the evidence clearly shows that it is simply a natural landform formed by geological processes over time. There are several reasons why the Face should be considered a natural feature rather than evidence of alien activity. First, analyses have shown that the shadows and lighting in the original images make the rocks appear more face-like than they really are. Upon closer inspection by spacecraft and with better lighting conditions, the geometric patterns that resembled facial features became less distinct. This suggests that trickery of perception, rather than design by intelligent lifeforms, best explains its face-like appearance. Second, studies of the geological structures in the area have found similar patterns and formations that are undoubtedly natural. The layered rock strata and erosion visible in other parts of the Colonia region prove that natural weathering over millions of years can carve mesa-like plateaus with varying elevations and slopes. Geologists recognize the "Face" as conforming to these natural patterns rather than intelligent design. Finally, the lack of archaeological or artificial materials discovered provides further evidence that it was not constructed by aliens. If visitors from another world had shaped the rocks into a gigantic face, we would expect to find evidence of the tools, machinery, or artificial materials used. However, chemical and spectral analysis has found only ordinary Martian bedrock and minerals. The absence of technological or artificially constructed traces makes an alien origin incredibly unlikely. In conclusion, while the concept of an alien-made "Face on Mars" captured people's imaginations for a time, scientific analysis shows that it is consistent with the geological structures naturally formed on Mars through erosion over eons. Unless compelling new evidence is discovered, such as artificial compounds or technology, the most reasonable conclusion is that it is simply a chance product of planetary geology rather than alien visitation or communication. The facts support classifying it as a natural landform rather than a sign of extraterrestrial intelligence.

The convenience of having a car drive itself could exacerbate this issue, leading to a disconnection from the act of driving and a lack of situational awareness. This could lead to wider socio-economic disparities and question the practicality of mass-producing vehicles that are not universally accessible. Finally, the legal and ethical challenges surrounding driverless cars are significant. In the event of technology failure resulting in accidents, the lines of liability blur. Is the driver, who is no longer in active control, responsible, or does the onus fall on the manufacturer? This grey area could lead to complex legal battles and moral dilemmas. In conclusion, while the technology behind driverless cars is impressive, the potential risks and negative impacts on society outweigh the benefits. We must be cautious in our approach to this technology and consider the long-term consequences of relying on machines to make critical decisions. By prioritizing safety, preserving human autonomy, and ensuring accessibility for all, we can create a better future for all.

Pathogens can rapidly evolve and adapt, and thereby avoid detection and neutralization by the immune system; however, multiple defense mechanisms have also evolved to recognize and neutralize pathogens. Even simple organisms like bacteria possess a complex array of defense mechanisms that can recognize, trap, and neutralize foreign molecules. These include the production of antibodies, secretion of antimicrobial peptides, and restriction modification systems. More complex organisms, such as plants and animals, have developed additional defense mechanisms such as the adaptive immune system. This sophisticated system utilizes specialized cells, called lymphocytes, to recognize and destroy pathogens. Additionally, some organisms also mount a physical barrier against invading microbes by secreting mucus or forming a cell wall. Finally, certain species of bacteria produce toxins that can kill other microbial invaders. In summary, numerous defense mechanisms exist to protect organisms from pathogenic invaders. These range from the production of antibodies to the formation of physical barriers, and even to the production of toxins by some species of bacteria.

MapReduce is a popular programming paradigm for developing large-scale, data-intensive computation. Many frameworks that implement this paradigm have recently been developed. To leverage these frameworks, however, developers must become familiar with the programming model they impose. This is a barrier to adoption, and can lead to programs that are difficult to maintain. We propose a novel approach to programming MapReduce-like computations, which does not require familiarity with the underlying programming model. The programmer specifies the computation in terms of a sequence of relational queries (with nested sub-queries), and the system automatically generates the required MapReduce programs. We have implemented our approach in a system called Quill, which we have used to implement a wide range of data analysis tasks. Our evaluation demonstrates that Quill significantly improves programmer productivity.

TL:DR: You should read something like The Little Book of Common Sense Investing, and read some of the popular questions on this site. The main message that you will get from that research is that there is an inescapable connection between risk and reward, or to put it another way, volatility and reward. Things like government bonds and money market accounts have quite low risk, but also low reward. They offer a nearly guaranteed 1-3%. Stocks, high-risk bonds, or business ventures (like your soda and vending machine scheme) may return 20% a year some years, but you could also lose money, maybe all you've invested (e.g., what if a vandal breaks one of your machines or the government adds a $5 tax for each can of soda?). Research has shown that the best way for the normal person to use their money to make money is to buy index funds (these are funds that buy a bunch of different stocks), and to hold them for a long time (over 10-15 years). By buying a broad range of stocks, you avoid some of the risks of investing (e.g., if one company's stock tanks, you don't lose very much), while keeping most of the benefits. By keeping them for a long time, the good years more than even out the bad years, and you are almost guaranteed to make ~6-7%/year. Buying individual stocks is a really, really bad idea. If you aren't willing to invest the time to become an expert investor, then you will almost certainly do worse than index funds over the long run. Another option is to use your capital to start a side business (like your vending machine idea). As mentioned before, this still has risks. One of those risks is that it will take more work than you expect (who will find places for your vending machines? Who will fill them? Who will hire those who fill them? etc.). The great thing about an index fund is that it doesn't take work or research. However, if there are things that you want to do, that take capital, this can be a good way to make more income.

Historical fiction is a genre of literature that uses real historical events and people as the basis for a fictional story. It is a popular genre, with many famous novels such as The Three Musketeers, The Scarlet Letter, and War and Peace falling into the category. However, the historical accuracy of historical fiction is often debated. Some critics argue that historical fiction is inherently inaccurate, as it is impossible to recreate the past perfectly. Others argue that historical fiction can be accurate, as long as the author does their research and stays true to the historical record. There are a number of factors that contribute to the historical accuracy of historical fiction. One important factor is the author's research. The author must have a deep understanding of the historical period in which their novel is set. This includes knowledge of the political, social, and cultural events of the time, as well as the lives of the people who lived during that time. If the author does not have a good understanding of the historical period, their novel will likely be inaccurate. Another important factor is the author's ability to create believable characters. The characters in a historical novel must be believable and relatable, even if they are based on real historical figures. The author must be able to capture the essence of the characters' personalities and motivations, and make them feel like real people. If the characters are not believable, the novel will not be convincing, and readers will not be able to connect with the story. Finally, the author's writing style can also contribute to the historical accuracy of a novel. The author must use language that is appropriate for the time period in which the novel is set. They must also be able to create a vivid and believable setting. If the writing style is not appropriate for the time period, the novel will not be convincing, and readers will not be able to immerse themselves in the story. In conclusion, the historical accuracy of historical fiction is a complex issue. There are a number of factors that contribute to the accuracy of a novel, including the author's research, their ability to create believable characters, and their writing style. If an author can do all of these things, they can write a historical novel that is both accurate and entertaining.

Apple Corporation’s Production Analysis Essay Apple is a corporation that has been around for many years and creates products known to many people worldwide. Apple has created many products, including phones, tablets, and laptops, which are widely used nowadays. As one of the most well-known and effective brands in its marketing, Apple, located in a core country of the United States, must find financially efficient solutions for its production and sales. The production of Apple Corporation, a company that began in the United States of America, has been taking place in China for many years. The labor force in China is relatively cheaper to manufacture than in the United States, as the cost of labor, sourcing of materials, supplies, and much more is reduced. This is due, firstly, to the size of the population, and secondly, to the education and qualifications available. Labor costs in China have always been somewhat lower, especially in medium-sized cities (Naftali, 2021). Thus, it is profitable for Apple to use China as a production site in order to reduce costs. This allows Apple to pay average wages to its employees, ship goods wholesale to different countries from a convenient location in China, and sell in countries around the world where demand for Apple products is high. At the same time, the production of electronics in China is at a very high level, which allows for maintaining the quality standard required by Apple. This shows how developed companies use periphery or semi-periphery states for their own purposes. Such use of other countries allows to reduce costs, but at the same time, it is not an objective sign of national discrimination since, thanks to Apple’s factories, it creates many jobs in China. In conclusion, the fact that Apple provides jobs eliminates the question of unethical news, as Apple uses China as a cost-effective solution to optimize production. Companies that exist and operate in a competitive market of electronic gadgets and other goods are forced to compete with each other and minimize costs for financial efficiency. Apple uses resources from different countries to fully optimize the processes. Reference Naftali, O.
