World wide road traffic fatality and accident rates are high, and this is true even in technologically advanced countries like the USA. Despite the advances in Intelligent Trans- portation Systems, safe transportation routing i.e., finding safest routes is largely an overlooked paradigm. In recent years, large amount of traffic data has been produced by people, Internet of Vehicles and Internet of Things (IoT). Also, thanks to advances in cloud computing and proliferation of mobile communication technologies, it is now possible to perform analysis on vast amount of generated data (crowd sourced) and deliver the result back to users in real time. This paper proposes SafeRNet, a safe route computation framework which takes advantage of these technologies to analyze streaming traffic data and historical data to effectively infer safe routes and deliver them back to users in real time. SafeRNet utilizes Bayesian network to formulate safe route model. Furthermore, a case study is presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using real traffic data. SafeRNet intends to improve drivers' safety in a modern technology rich transportation system.

I disagree with making extracurricular activities mandatory for all students. While activities can benefit many, others may have good reasons not to participate that should be respected. Nequiring extracurriculars leaves out important differences among individuals. Not all enjoy the same activities or have the same abilities, interests or availability outside of school. Some may need time for jobs, family duties or other commitments. Forcing participation risks damaging self esteem if students feel unable to succeed or simply dislike an assigned activity. Extracurriculars are best if students freely choose them according to their passions. This fosters intrinsic motivation and makes the most of each person's talents. Those passionate about an activity will do best and gain the intended benefits of things like teamwork, time management and leadership skills. Others forced to participate lag or halfhearted go through the motions without learning as much. A mandatory policy also misses that downtime is important for rest, private pursuits and individual growth. Not every minute needs to be scheduled. Unstructured free time allows for reflection, creativity and personal responsibility over scheduling. Too many demands risks burnout, especially for high achieving or struggling students juggling academic requirements. Instead of requirements, the school would better support varied student interests through diverse extracurricular options and encouraging participation without pressure. Those seeking new experiences or skills are free to choose from many appealing clubs and sports, while others can prioritize as works best for their lives. This preserves individual freedom and respects that learning happens through many paths. In conclusion, while extracurricular activities offer valuable benefits, requiring participation against some students' wills risks damaging motivation, confidence and work life balance. Students thrive most when able to freely explore diverse options and priorities according to their own needs and passions. The school should support involvement, not mandate it uniformly for all.

When we are managing a large number of things , we like to organize them in groups of some power of 10 : I 'm gon na buy * * 1 * * TV ( 10 ^ 0 ) , * * 10 * * boxes ( 10 ^ 1 ) , * * 100 * * apples ( 10 ^ 2 ) , * * 1,000 * * songs ( 10 ^ 3 ) , etc . It 's just easier for us to keep track of a large number of things by grouping them this way ( what 's easier to remember : 8,723 donuts , or 8 groups of 1,000 donuts ? ) . This is because our numbering system is something called " base 10 , " meaning we think of all of numberdom in terms of 10 . A simple count of the fingers on our hands explains why we made this so . Computers , on the other hand , think in base 2 ( each bit is either on or off , only two states ) . While we like to group things in powers of 10 , computers feel most comfortable grouping things in powers of 2 . If a computer were to group boxes together , it 'd be in groups like * * 1 * * ( 2 ^ 0 ) , * * 2 * * ( 2 ^ 1 ) , * * 4 * * ( 2 ^ 2 ) , * * 8 * * ( 2 ^ 3 ) , ... , * * 256 * * ( 2 ^ 8 ) , * * 512 * * ( 2 ^ 9 ) , * * 1024 * * ( 2 ^ 10 ) , * * 2048 * * ( 2 ^ 11 ) , etc . Those numbers just make " sense " to the computer just like how 100 , 1000 , etc just make " sense " to humans , and it allows the computer to access and use all of that memory in efficient ways and keep track of all of it easily . With the rapid increase in volume of time series medical data available through wearable devices, there is a need to employ automated algorithms to label data. Examples of labels include interventions, changes in activity (e.g. sleep) and changes in physiology (e.g. arrhythmias). However, automated algorithms tend to be unreliable resulting in lower quality care. Expert annotations are scarce, expensive, and prone to significant inter- and intra-observer variance. To address these problems, a Bayesian Continuous-valued Label Aggregator (BCLA) is proposed to provide a reliable estimation of label aggregation while accurately infer the precision and bias of each algorithm. The BCLA was applied to QT interval (pro-arrhythmic indicator) estimation from the electrocardiogram using labels from the 2006 PhysioNetComputing in Cardiology Challenge database. It was compared to the mean, median, and a previously proposed Expectation Maximization (EM) label aggregation approaches. While accurately predicting each labelling algorithm's bias and precision, the root-mean-square error of the BCLA was 11.78 0.63ms, significantly outperforming the best Challenge entry (15.37 2.13ms) as well as the EM, mean, and median voting strategies (14.76 0.52ms, 17.61 0.55ms, and 14.43 0.57ms respectively with p 0.0001). The BCLA could therefore provide accurate estimation for medical continuous-valued label tasks in an unsupervised manner even when the ground truth is not available.

Video Object Segmentation (VOS) is an active research area of the visual domain. One of its fundamental sub-tasks is semi-supervised one-shot learning: given only the segmentation mask for the first image, it is expected to provide the segmentation mask for the second image. However, this task is extremely difficult for both human annotators and machine learning algorithms due to the lack of ground truth information for the second image. To tackle this problem, we propose an automatic pseudo ground truth estimation algorithm, which utilizes the consistency between different masks of the same object in different images. We construct the object mask consistency matrix by computing the correspondence between different masks of the same object in different images. Then, we use the Kruskal algorithm to obtain the optimal shortest path that leads to the most consistent masks. In our experiment, the algorithm achieves a 0.753 F-score in the one-shot learning of the Pascal VOC 2012 challenge dataset. Huang, Hengdong, "Automatic Pseudo Ground Truth Estimation for Video Object Segmentation" (2017). Computer Science - Dissertations. 133.

The Influence of Television on Consumerism: A Comprehensive Analysis Television, as a dominant medium of mass communication, has significantly shaped and influenced the consumer behavior of individuals across the globe. Consumerism, in its essence, is the behavior of individuals and groups as they seek to acquire and consume goods and services. This paper will delve into the relationship between television and consumerism, examining the various ways in which television has shaped and influenced consumer behavior, attitudes, and societal norms. Television, as an influential medium, provides marketers with an opportunity to reach vast audiences through advertisements. The content of television programs often reflects the values and ideals of the society, which in turn shapes consumer behavior. For instance, advertising campaigns during popular television shows can influence viewers to purchase specific products or services, thereby promoting consumerism. One of the primary ways television influences consumerism is through the portrayal of consumer culture in various TV shows and movies. These depictions often showcase the lifestyles of affluent individuals, encouraging viewers to aspire to a certain lifestyle, thereby driving the demand for luxury goods and services. Moreover, television series often feature product placement, where products are intentionally placed in scenes to promote their use and increase sales. Television also impacts consumerism through its ability to influence societal norms and values. Shows that depict materialism and consumer culture as central themes can shape the perceptions of viewers, leading them to believe that the pursuit of material possessions is essential for happiness and fulfillment. This, in turn, can lead to increased consumer spending. Furthermore, television has the power to create trends and set fashion standards. Reality TV shows and fashion-themed programs often showcase the latest trends and styles, which can influence viewers to emulate these trends, thereby driving demand for specific products. This phenomenon is evident in the fashion industry, where television has played a significant role in shaping consumer preferences and trends. In conclusion, the influence of television on consumerism is undeniable. Through its ability to reach vast audiences, depict consumer culture, influence societal norms, and create trends, television plays a crucial role in shaping consumer behavior, attitudes, and societal values. As television continues to evolve and new platforms emerge, it will be essential to continue studying the effects of this powerful medium on consumerism and its impact on society as a whole.

Federated Learning enables entities to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model while keeping their training data locally. It prevents data collection and aggregation and, therefore, mitigates the associated privacy risks. However, it still remains vulnerable to various security attacks where malicious participants aim at degrading the generated model, inserting backdoors, or inferring other participants' training data. This paper presents a new federated learning scheme that provides different trade-offs between robustness, privacy, bandwidth efficiency, and model accuracy. Our scheme uses biased quantization of model updates and hence is bandwidth efficient. It is also robust against state-of-the-art backdoor as well as model degradation attacks even when a large proportion of the participant nodes are malicious. We propose a practical differentially private extension of this scheme which protects the whole dataset of participating entities. We show that this extension performs as efficiently as the non-private but robust scheme, even with stringent privacy requirements but are less robust against model degradation and backdoor attacks. This suggests a possible fundamental trade-off between Differential Privacy and robustness.

The Earth's atmosphere is like a giant balloon, with the air inside constantly moving around and trying to find a balance. When the air pressure is higher in one place, the air will try to move to an area with lower pressure to balance things out. So, in short, wind is caused by differences in air pressure and the movement of air to try and balance out these differences.

Established in the aftermath of World War II during the Bretton Woods Conference in 1944, the IMF's primary purpose was to promote international monetary cooperation, facilitate the expansion and balanced growth of international trade, and contribute thereby to the promotion and maintenance of high levels of employment and real income. It was also tasked with the establishment of a multilateral system of payments and the elimination of foreign exchange restrictions that might hamper the growth of world trade. The IMF's role in global economic stability can be likened to a guardian that oversees the financial well-being of its member countries by providing them with the tools necessary to prevent economic calamities. This entails a range of activities, including monitoring the economic and financial developments of countries and offering policy advice aimed at crisis prevention. Through its surveillance mechanism, the IMF assesses the financial health of its 190 member countries, highlighting potential risks to stability and advising on needed policy adjustments. A cornerstone of the IMF's stabilizing efforts is its financial assistance programs. When a country faces a balance of payments crisis--meaning it does not have enough reserves to cover its international obligations--the IMF can step in to provide temporary financial assistance. This aid is designed to provide a buffer that allows the country time to correct imbalances in its economy without resorting to measures that could have adverse effects domestically or internationally. The image, known as "Face on Mars" or "Cydonia Face," quickly became famous and inspired numerous theories, speculation, and even books. Some scientists argued that the formation was simply a natural geological formation, while others believed that it was a result of intelligent design, either by an extraterrestrial civilization or by a higher power that had created the face to send a signal. The most prominent theory was the "Ancient Alien" hypothesis, which proposed that the face was a structure built by an advanced civilization on Mars. Proponents argued that the face was a symbol, perhaps representing an ancient deity or a message to other civilizations in the universe. However, the scientific community remained skeptical, and further analysis revealed that the "Face on Mars" was likely a natural formation created by wind and weather over thousands of years. The face is located on the Martian surface, and the wind has carved out various shapes over time. As the years went by, more images and information were collected from Mars, and other similar formations were discovered. This led scientists to conclude that the face was nothing more than a geological anomaly, and the "Face on Mars" mystery was finally laid to rest. The Face on Mars is an interesting example of how a single image can spark curiosity, imagination, and scientific inquiry. Although the face turned out to be a natural formation, it continues to inspire people to look beyond our world in the search for answers to our existence and the mysteries of the universe.

French physicists have discovered a new kind of buoyancy produced through vibrating a medium. In experiments, the scientists found that highly viscous fluids levitated slightly above the bottom of an inverted air-filled chamber if the chamber was vibrating rapidly. This produced some interesting effects, with the scientists demonstrating that a toy boat could float upside down in a stable state on the underside of the levitating liquid. The discovery could have ripple effects in chemical engineering, where scientists use bubble filled columns as bioreactors.
